analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage in steps to $7.25 an hour by 2002.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: after referral to the House Education and the Workforce Committee in July 1997, it received no hearing, no vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the Fair Labor Standards Act to raise the federal minimum wage from the then-current level in five annual steps: $5.65 in 1998, $6.15 in 1999, $6.65 in 2000, $6.95 in 2001, and $7.25 in 2002 [S2][S3]. It was introduced by Rep. David Bonior with 23 cosponsors [S1][S4] and referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, which never acted on it [S1][S5]. It died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999 without ever reaching the House floor [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum wage — disproportionately adults in retail, food service, and other low-wage jobs — would see their hourly pay rise in five steps to $7.25 by 2002 [S2][S3]. Workers earning somewhat above the minimum often benefit too, as employers adjust pay scales upward.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in five annual steps from $5.65 (September 1998) to $7.25 (September 2002) [S2][S3].
The increase is written directly into the Fair Labor Standards Act's wage section, covering workers nationwide rather than leaving it to state action [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay minimum-wage workers — concentrated in restaurants, retail, agriculture, and other labor-intensive industries — would bear higher payroll costs, some of which typically pass through to consumers as slightly higher prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Restaurants, retail, and other low-wage employers

drawbacks.text: Employers of minimum-wage workers would face higher labor costs each year of the phase-in, and small businesses in low-margin industries would have to absorb them through higher prices, reduced hours, or fewer entry-level positions.

The schedule was fixed regardless of economic conditions; a downturn during the 1998–2002 phase-in would have forced the increases through anyway, since the bill contained no indexing or off-ramp [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A stepped federal minimum wage increase of this size directly raises pay for millions of the lowest-wage workers, which is its central purpose. The honest cost is borne by their employers and, in part, by consumers through prices, with the strongest good-faith concern being reduced entry-level hiring — though the evidence on that effect is genuinely contested. As drafted, the bill was simple and direct, but rigid; it built in no adjustment for economic conditions.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and sat there for the rest of the Congress without a hearing or vote, dying when the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Bonior introduced the bill on July 22, 1997, with Reps. Gephardt, Lewis of Georgia, Hinchey, Becerra, and Olver as original cosponsors [S1][S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day of introduction; that was the last formal action ever taken on it [S1][S5].
The sponsor gave introductory remarks on the House floor twice — July 23, 1997 and January 27, 1998 — but the committee never reported the bill and the House never voted on it [S5].
The bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999; no federal minimum wage increase along these lines was enacted during that Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay minimum-wage workers — restaurants, retail, and other labor-intensive industries — avoided the scheduled cost increases the bill would have imposed. Low-wage workers, meanwhile, received no federal raise from this bill during the 105th Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Minimum-wage employers; workers got no raise

for.name: Rep. David E. Bonior
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and promoted it in floor remarks in July 1997 and January 1998

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral in July 1997; never held a hearing, reported it out, or allowed a floor vote

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Controlled the House floor agenda in the 105th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was almost entirely Democratic — 22 of 23 cosponsors were Democrats plus one Independent — with no Republican cosponsors listed, and the Republican-controlled committee and House leadership never moved the bill [S4][S5].

industries.note: Among the most minimum-wage-dependent industries, it would have faced the steepest payroll cost increases from the step to $7.25 by 2002. Its interest in blocking the bill ran directly against the wage gains the bill offered low-wage workers.

A large share of retail pay sits at or near the minimum wage; the bill would have raised those labor costs in five steps. Its gain from the bill's death came at the cost of no raise for its lowest-paid workers.
The group the bill was written for — workers at or near the minimum wage — received nothing because the bill died; their interest ran entirely with passage.
